newsitem.title: USA: As strong U.S. spurs dlr, Fed hike bets overdone.
newsitem.headline: As strong U.S. spurs dlr, Fed hike bets overdone.

text.p: The juxtaposition of swelling U.S. non-farm payrolls against disappointing German jobless data last week helped catapult the dollar to a fresh 29-month high of 1.5925 marks on Monday.
The strong U.S. data fanned the belief that investors will be unable to resist the relative allure of the U.S. economy.

But as traders zero-in on the major technical target at 1.60 marks, some analysts wondered whether the market has priced into the dollar exchange rate a bigger interest rate hike than the Federal Reserve will likely deliver.

"I think we have a hard time sustaining a move above 1.60 until we see signs that growth here is strong enough to really trigger more than one 25-basis-point tightening," said Richard Koss, international strategist at MFR Inc, an investment advisory firm.
Koss called "premature" many forecasts calling for two or three tightenings during the course of 1997.
Extending a string of gains which have advanced it 3.3 percent since the beginning of the year, the dollar muscled it's way past 1.59 marks on Monday, reaching 1.5925, its highest since August 1994.
"It's sort of like the stock market," said Randolph Donney, director of capital markets at consulting firm Pegasus Econometrics Group. "You just wonder how much there can be."
On Friday, the U.S. Labor Department reported the economy produced 262,000 new jobs in December.

This sent yields on U.S. Treasury bonds to their highest level in more than 3-months, reflecting heightened speculation that the Fed might administer a rate increase to prevent a tight labor market from generating increased wage inflation.
Higher U.S. interest rates make dollar-denominated financial instruments more attractive to investors.

At 5.3 percent, the December U.S. unemployment rate is already well below the level at which many economists predict workers will be able to demand higher wages from employers confronting a shortage of job seekers.

Meanwhile, as if to punctuate a year of disappointing economic growth with an exclamation point, Germany reported on Thursday the number of jobless rose 48,000 in December, while it's rate of unemployment jumped to 10.9 percent from 10.3 in November.
"Better-than-expected employment in the U.S., worse than expected in Germany -- you couldn't have better divergence in economic indicators right now for the dollar," Donney said.
"Even though it may look a little frothy, it's hard to get your arms around a short position at this stage," he added.
Koss said some in the U.S. bond and currency market were expecting just a quarter percent or slightly greater tightening by the middle of the year.
German markets have priced in a very slight decrease in interest rates from the Bundesbank, Germany's central bank, economists said.
But experts said the U.S. economy provides little foundation for market bets the central bank will commence a cycle of credit tightenings this year, after laying dormant for much of 1996.
The consumer, for instance, which represents two-thirds of U.S. economic activity, seems to have delivered retailers a particularly disappointing Christmas shopping season.
"If we do get some signs of consumer demand staying at best modest, you might get some signs of a correction (in bond market) later in the first quarter," Koss said.

The last time the Fed adjusted interest rates was January 1996, when it trimmed short-term rates by one quarter percent. The federal funds target rate, which banks charge each other for overnight loans, has remained at 5.25 percent and the discount rate at 5.0 percent since that cut almost a year ago.

"Speculation of Fed tightening, speculation of Bundesbank easing -- that kind of sentiment is going to prevail for the next two, three, four weeks. And in that time frame, we are certainly going to test 1.60 (marks) and could even go higher," said Earl Johnson, foreign exchange economist at Bank of Montreal.
"The interesting question is: what if we don't raise and what if they don't cut? And I frankly don't think either one is going to happen," Johnson said.
